podcast.title: "Suzy Q" Musical Synthesis
podcast.body: The song "Suzy Q" was a blend of various musical sources; its overall sound was influenced by Muddy Waters' "Baby Please Don't Go," its melody by The Clovers, and its guitar riff by Howlin' Wolf, suggesting it evolved from jam sessions despite conflicting authorship claims. "The most obvious influence for its overall sound. Both the melody and the way the melody interacts with the guitar riff. Is Baby Please Don't Go by Marty Waters."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: "Suzy Q" Songwriting Credit Discrepancy
podcast.body: Hawkins claimed that not only were the songwriting credits for "Suzy Q" wrongly attributed (to Stan Lewis and Delna Roadwater), but he also did not receive any royalties until 1985. Crucially, co-writers like James Burton received no credit. "But according to Hawkins, not only did the credit get split with the wrong people, but he didn't receive any of the royalties to which he was entitled until as late as 1985."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Academic Achievement
podcast.body: In the early 1980s, after getting clean, Hawkins achieved a significant personal milestone by earning his master's degree, an accomplishment he was as proud of as any hit record, especially considering he was a high school dropout. "as well as finally getting his master's degree, which for a high school dropout was a major achievement and something to be as proud of as any hit."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Amphetamine Addiction and Recovery
podcast.body: Hawkins battled an amphetamine addiction throughout much of the 1970s, having started using speed in the 1950s. He successfully got clean in the early 1980s, subsequently performing on the Rockabilly Revival circuit. "But after a successful few years, he spent much of the 70s suffering from an emphetamine addiction, having started taking speed back in the 50s."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Chess Records' Delayed Release of "Suzy Q"
podcast.body: Chess Records inexplicably delayed the release of "Suzy Q" for 10 months after receiving the master. Hawkins, frustrated, sent a copy to Jerry Wexler at Atlantic Records, who expressed interest, which then prompted Chess to recognize its commercial potential and finally release it on Checker. "What's surprising is how reluctant chests were to release the single."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Country Music Family Background
podcast.body: Hawkins came from a country music family; his father, Dalmar Hawkins Sr, was a country musician and bass player, possibly an original member of the Sons of the Pioneers, and his younger brother Jerry was a rockabilly who released singles in the 1950s. Despite this, Dale felt he lacked the country element necessary for the rockabilly label. "His father, Dalmar Horkin's senior, was a country musician who was, according to some sources, one of the original members of the sons of the pioneers, the group that launched the Come Here."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Credited Record Production
podcast.body: After his TV show, Hawkins transitioned into record production for Stan Lewis's new labels. He is credited as the producer for the hit song "Do It Again Just a Little Bit Slower" by John & Robin, though claims of producing Bruce Channel's "Hey Baby" and John Fred and His Playboy Band's "Judy in Disguise (With Glasses)" are uncredited. "On the other hand, he is the credited producer on the big hit. Do it again just a little bit slower by John and Robin."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Early Connection to Hank Williams
podcast.body: Hawkins' early musical collaborator, Sonny Jones, was a local guitarist whose sister was the widow of Hank Williams, providing Jones with valuable contacts in the local music industry that helped Hawkins form his first band. "Jones had a lot of contacts in the local music industry and how Hawkins pulled together the first line-up of his band when he was 19."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Head of A&R at RCA Records
podcast.body: After his late 1960s recording comeback was unsuccessful, Hawkins moved to RCA Records to become the head of A&R for their West Coast rock department, a position reportedly recommended to him by Jo-El Sonnier. "When that wasn't a success, he moved on to RCA Records to become head of A&R for their West Coast rock department, a job he was apparently put forward for by Joaz Boran."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Louisiana Hayride Parking Scheme
podcast.body: Hawkins' initial job at the Louisiana Hayride was not as a performer but working in the car park. He and his brother charged drivers 50 cents for parking, but they failed to disclose that the car park was actually free to the public. "What they didn't tell the drivers was that the car park was actually free to the public."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Name Change to "Del Hawkins"
podcast.body: During the release of "See You Soon, Baboon," Chess Records' Leonard Chess misheard "Dale Hawkins" over the phone, leading to his first name being misspelled as "Del" on the record. This spelling then became his professional name from that point forward. "Leonard Chess misheard Del Hawkins over the phone, and the record came out as by Del Hawkins, which would be his name from that point on."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Paradoxical Musical Legacy
podcast.body: Dale Hawkins is considered a paradoxical figure: he foresaw the future of rock and roll where white artists adapted black blues ideas, yet his own biggest hit, "Suzy Q," was meticulously crafted from various musical fragments, despite his reputation for raw, instinctive rock and roll. "He was in many ways a paradoxical figure."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Pioneering Electric Bass Use in Rock and Roll
podcast.body: For the released version of "Suzy Q," Hawkins consciously chose an electric bass, played by Sonny Tramble (the only person in Shreveport to own one), to emulate the sound of electric blues records, differentiating it from the double bass typically associated with country and rockabilly music. "This was a deliberate choice by Hawkins, who wanted to imitate the sound of electric blues records, rather than using the double bass, which he associated with country music."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Presaging 1960s White Rock Acts
podcast.body: Dale Hawkins is argued to be a pivotal figure, possibly the first white rock and roller to be directly inspired by black blues musicians like Muddy Waters and Howlin' Wolf. His song "Suzy Q," with its electric bass, Chess-style guitar riffs, and country-inflected vocals, is considered a precursor to 1960s white rock acts like The Rolling Stones and The Animals. "One can make an argument that Dale Hawkins was the first white Wuck and Ruler to be inspired by people like Waters and Wolf, and for Susie Q as the record, more than any other, that presaged the white rock acts of the 60s."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Record Shop Expertise and Friendships
podcast.body: While beginning his music career, Hawkins worked at Stan's Record Shop, where he became deeply familiar with nearly every blues and R&B record available. This job also led to a lifelong friendship with customers like B.B. King. "It was through doing this job that Hawkins became friendly with customers like Bibi King, who would remain a lifelong friend."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Self-Identified Bluesman
podcast.body: Dale Hawkins consistently thought of himself as a bluesman, rather than a rockabilly, a description he disliked. While living in Shreveport, Louisiana, he resided in a shack in the black part of town, possessing only a folding camp bed, a record player, and thousands of 78 RPM blues records. "When he was living in Shreveport, Louisiana, he lived in a shack in the black part of town, and inside the shack there was only a folding camp bed, a record player, and thousands of 78 RPM blues records."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: The Dale Hawkins Show TV Series
podcast.body: Following his initial string of hits, Hawkins leveraged his connection with Dick Clark of "American Bandstand" to secure his own television program, "The Dale Hawkins Show." This show ran for 18 months and followed a format similar to "American Bandstand." "he used his connection with Dick Clark, the TV presenter whose American bandstand had helped to break Suzy Kew on the national market to get his own TV show, The Dale Hawkins Show, which ran for 18 months and was a similar format to the bandstand."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
